 North Of North Season 2 Is The New Gold Standard For Heartwarming, Culturally Immersive Comedy | Review
 Anna Lambe as Siaja Kudlak and Zorga Qaunaq as Millie Maktaana in North of North season 2 
 Back on Netflix this November, Inuit sitcom North of North is even better this time around, setting a new benchmark for culturally immersive comedy.

 North of North is back on Netflix, giving Inuk single mother Siaja Kudlak (Anna Lambe) the welcome return to streaming she so richly deserves. Siaja’s story is even more compelling this time around, in a sitcom season that’s beautifully paced and packed full of terrific, culturally insightful subplots, both comedic and tragic.

 The ending to North of North season 1 left us reeling from the revelation that the show’s protagonist has an older half-sister who was taken away from her mother as a young child. This storyline echoes the harrowing experiences of real-life Inuit parents, who have faced generations of separation from their children in Canada and elsewhere, in large part due to the residual vestiges of colonial oppression and institutional racism.
 Elsewhere, Siaja’s father, played by Jay Ryan, had decided to stay in the remote Arctic town of Ice Cove where she, her mother, and her daughter all live. As had her primary love interest, Kuuk, although his culturally insensitive white British Columbian girlfriend was coming up to live with him.
 Although Ice Cove is a fictional place, it’s based on actual Inuit communities in the Canadian territory of Nunavut, and North of North ’s filming locations around the territory’s capital city Iqaluit reflect the real lives of these communities. In the show’s second season, we get a sense of just how brutally harsh the living conditions this far into the Arctic Circle can be when winter sets in.
 North Of North Is Now Netflix’s Best Sitcom
 North of North protagonist smiling 
 It’s not for nothing that North of North has achieved back-to-back Rotten Tomatoes scores of 100%, setting a new record for a Netflix sitcom. In season 2, the series doubles down on its earthy combination of flawed but well-meaning characters, side-splitting social farce, and piercing cultural insight.
 We see Siaja, her mother Neevee (Maika Harper), her father Alistair, and the man her heart truly belongs to, Kuuk (Braeden Clarke), all grow in unexpected ways, which nonetheless feel authentic to their characterizations. Siaja’s older sister, Olivia, is also introduced to us, through a painfully realistic sequence of events that leaves North of North with plenty more to explore in a third season it’s already earned several times over.
 This season is the best sitcom release of 2026, and deserves its day in the winter sun.
 The show isn’t all weighty family drama, though. Siaja’s boss, Ice Cove’s non-Inuk town manager Helen (Mary Lynn Rajskub), continues to deliver consistent laughs with vainglorious statements about her own achievements, reflecting her woefully misguided sense of self-importance when it comes to stewarding the community’s resources. She’s joined in this season by Alexis, Kuuk’s white, matcha latte-sipping TikTok influencer who revels in the appropriation of Inuit culture.
 North of North strikes the perfect balance between comedy, culturally-specific personal struggles, and inspirational small-town heroism. It’s a credit to creators and showrunners Stacey Aglok MacDonald and Alethea Arnaquq-Baril that they’ve managed to come at traditional sitcom tropes from a new angle with refreshing sincerity, while fully immersing us in the story world they’ve constructed.
 There’s a chance that further seasons may get a little repetitive if the series doesn’t broaden its scope slightly, and Siaja’s trip to Toronto suggests we may see more of the big city in next year’s episodes. In any case, North of North ’s second season is the best sitcom release of 2026, and deserves its day in the winter sun.
 Neevee’s Character Growth Is Season 2’s Strongest Point
 One of the best things about this new season is the growth of Siaja’s mother Neevee as a character. A battle-hardened single mother in her own right, she’s defined by her no-nonsense approach to family and aversion to her own feelings throughout season 1, and much of season 2.
 Neevee and Siaja have a complex relationship in North of North , which is only complicated further by the revelation that Siaja has a half-sister her mother has been hiding from her. Siaja’s efforts to track down her long-lost sibling constitute the emotional crux of season 2. Yet it’s Neevee’s reaction when Siaja’s trip to meet Olivia ends in disaster that ultimately seals the season’s tearjerking credentials.
 It’s an unexpected joy to see Neevee fighting Siaja’s corner so fiercely.
 The deep, unconditional embrace she gives Siaja when she finds out what her daughter has done – against her wishes – provides a powerful ending to the season’s sixth episode. But it’s three scenes in subsequent episodes that really show us how much Neevee has grown as a person.
 First, there’s her insistence on bringing Siaja’s father to comfort his daughter, despite her own difficult relationship with him. Then, there’s the heart-to-heart she shares with Siaja out in the snow, where she finally tells her daughter to follow her instincts. Perhaps most impressively of all, Neevee stands up to Siaja’s boss for her, and asserts her own position as Siaja’s mother in a way she’s never done before.

 “I’m her mother ,” she tells Helen. “You’re her boss. Let’s not confuse paychecks with parenting. ” When she accuses Helen of only valuing Siaja because “ she makes you look good ,” she even manages to elicit some praise out of her. " She is good ,” Helen admits for the first time. “ Better than she knows. I just don't want her to lose everything she's worked for this year .”
 It’s an unexpected joy to see Neevee fighting Siaja’s corner so fiercely. Her growth as a parent will surely continue in season 3, when we’re all hoping she gets to meet her other daughter, Olivia, for the first time since she was a child.
 Ice Cove Is More Heartwarming Than Ever In Season 2
 From the traditional uaajeerneq mask dance of season 2’s first episode, to the winter ball Siaja and her friends put on for the season finale, Ice Cove does even more to warm our hearts this winter than it did in North of North ’s first season. Millie and Colin are a source of boundless good vibes, Kuuk’s growth into a school teacher is even more adorable than the way he looks at Siaja, and the town’s Inuit elders deliver their own fair share of deadpan hilarity.
 All in all, this new season of Netflix’s indigenous Arctic sitcom is an unqualified triumph, which charms us at every turn. There are very few shows out there like North of North , so we should cherish it for as long as it lasts.
 Where the show’s second season truly exceeds itself is best encapsulated by the Inuit concept pilimmaksarniq , which roughly translates as “ forging yourself into what you want to become ”, as tribal elder Auntie Vicky explains in its first episode. While she’s referring to Siaja’s personal journey, the term applies to North of North ’s storytelling as a whole. The series is forging a powerful legacy for itself, and every Netflix subscriber should be there to witness it.
 All episodes of North of North season 2 are now streaming on Netflix. 
 9 /10
